name: rscrypto
baseline: RustCrypto sha2/sha3/blake2 crates (fastest external Rust crypto crate per case, across an 8-host CI matrix)
workload: Criterion benchmarks of one-shot/streaming SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA3-224/256/384/512, and BLAKE2b/BLAKE2s hashing, run across 8 Linux hosts (x86_64 AMD/Intel, aarch64, ppc64le, s390x, riscv64) plus Windows x86_64 AMD/Intel
claimed_speedup: Fastest-external geomean (rscrypto_time is the denominator, so >1x = rscrypto faster): sha256 1.27x (median 1.60x), sha384 1.30x, sha512 1.29x, sha3-224 2.27x, sha3-256 2.28x, sha3-384 2.35x, sha3-512 2.38x, blake2b256 1.07x (median 1.31x), blake2b512 1.08x (median 1.33x), blake2s256 1.11x, blake2s128 1.13x
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.98.1 on native x86_64/aarch64 CI runners; Rust 1.99.0-nightly (3d6c19bb9, 2026-08-11) for cross-built powerpc64le/s390x/riscv64; Criterion harness, release profile
hardware: 8-host AWS matrix: c8a.2xlarge (x86_64 AMD), c8i.2xlarge (x86_64 Intel), c9g.2xlarge (aarch64), native powerpc64le/s390x/riscv64 runners, plus Windows x86_64 AMD/Intel c8a/c8i.2xlarge (per the 2026-08-18 eight-host Linux scorecard referenced in the same document)
tradeoffs: Rust-only, no_std feature-gated, zero default OpenSSL/system-lib dependency; baseline is other Rust crates, not the OpenSSL C library itself.
caveats: Baseline is the fastest competing Rust crate (RustCrypto sha2/sha3/blake2), not OpenSSL's own C implementation, so baseline_in_list is false. The same OVERVIEW.md document explicitly withdraws unrelated ML-KEM and Argon2 comparisons for methodology problems (mixed entropy/salt handling); the sha2/sha3/blake2 rows used here are from the separate 2026-08-18 eight-host Linux scorecard and are not among the withdrawn rows, but the document's history of retracted claims warrants caution.

name: sha256mb
workload: Batched SHA-256 over n=6144 independent 33-byte compressed secp256k1 public keys (64-byte stride), GOMAXPROCS=1, arm64 hardware-SHA (sha2x4) backend vs scalar crypto/sha256
claimed_speedup: ~2.6x faster than scalar crypto/sha256 on Apple M3 (57.6M vs 21.6M hashes/s at n=6144; 2.57-2.67x across thermal states); README smoke table gives scalar = 21,550,000 hashes/s, 711.8 MB/s at the same batch size
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.22.5, GOMAXPROCS=1, go test -bench -benchmem -count=8, median of runs
tradeoffs: Only the arm64 backend is vectorized (ARMv8 SHA256H/H2/SU0/SU1 4-lane interleave); amd64 has no SIMD backend yet and runs scalar. Requires a batched, fixed-33-byte-message workload (compressed pubkeys) to see the win; a single ad-hoc SHA-256 call gets no speedup.
caveats: Extremely new project, 0 stars, single author, no independent verification; numbers are a 'local smoke benchmark' by the author rather than a CI-tracked series; narrow workload (33-byte keys) may not generalize to arbitrary message sizes.

name: hashtree
workload: Batched SHA-256 compression of many 64-byte blocks per call (1/4/8/16 blocks at once) for Merkle-tree / beacon-chain hashing, built with HAVE_OPENSSL=1 to benchmark directly against OpenSSL's native SHA-256
claimed_speedup: On a CPU without SHA extensions: OpenSSL 30.519ms vs this library's avx_x8 (8 blocks/call) 6.519ms, about 4.7x faster (derived from page data); separately, on a Cascade Lake AVX-512 host, the avx_x16 kernel is ~12x faster than the library's own single-block implementation (not a same-run OpenSSL ratio)
compiler_and_flags: gcc/gas on Linux, Apple clang on Apple Silicon; built via `HAVE_OPENSSL=1 make all`; no explicit optimization flags stated
hardware: Unspecified x86-64 CPU described only as 'does not support SHA extensions' for the direct OpenSSL comparison; a separate Cascade Lake (AVX-512) x86 host and a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (ARMv8/NEON) for other rows
stars_or_usage: 42 stars; used in Ethereum consensus-layer client tooling for beacon-chain SSZ hashing (e.g. Prysm's gohashtree bindings)
tradeoffs: Only wins when many independent 64-byte blocks (Merkle-tree leaves) can be hashed together; a single hash call is no faster than OpenSSL. Requires SIMD (AVX2/AVX-512/SHA-NI/NEON). Low-level C API (raw pointers, fixed sizes, no bounds checking); caller owns all buffers.
caveats: The headline 4.7x-vs-OpenSSL number comes from a CPU whose exact model is not named in the README (only 'does not support SHA extensions'); the more specific Cascade Lake and Raspberry Pi benchmark rows do not include a same-run OpenSSL column, so the strongest per-CPU numbers and the direct-OpenSSL number are not from the same hardware.

name: libsodium (BLAKE2b)
workload: BLAKE2b one-shot hashing of 64/256/1024/4096/16384-byte buffers using Google Benchmark, with Crypto++ 8.9.0, OpenSSL 3.6.0, Botan 3.9.0, libsodium 1.0.20 and mbedTLS 4.0.0 all statically linked and built with identical compiler flags
claimed_speedup: libsodium's BLAKE2b beats OpenSSL's BLAKE2b at small-to-medium sizes: ~2.70x at 64B (577.8 vs 213.7 MB/s), ~1.91x at 256B (1243.6 vs 650.3 MB/s), ~1.18x at 1024B (1307.0 vs 1107.2 MB/s), about tied at 4096B (1338.4 vs 1333.9 MB/s); OpenSSL retakes the lead by ~4% at 16384B (1402.7 vs 1349.3 MB/s) (all derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto -funroll-loops -fomit-frame-pointer, static linking of all libraries built from source (per repo README); exact compiler and version are not recorded inside the result.json artifact itself
hardware: Host 'sccdeMacBook-Air.local', 8 logical CPUs, 32KB L1D / 128KB L1I / 4MB L2 per the result.json context block; the specific Apple Silicon chip model is not named
tradeoffs: libsodium's crypto_generichash BLAKE2b API differs from OpenSSL's EVP interface; the advantage shrinks and reverses as the buffer grows past ~8KB, so it is a small-message win rather than an across-the-board one.
caveats: This is a harvested shootout result (libsodium is the per-row winner vs OpenSSL for BLAKE2b at most sizes in this suite), not a claim libsodium itself makes. Single local run (dated 2025-11-05 in the artifact) by the benchmark author on a MacBook Air, not a multi-host CI matrix; exact CPU model and compiler version are not recorded in the JSON, only the flags in the README.
